canonical_topic: Electrical flow follows physics, not operator intent (loop flow / congestion)
definition: Power moves along the path(s) of least electrical resistance across the whole grid, not necessarily along the direct contractual path, so a grid operator must ensure spare capacity on every line the power could conceivably flow across.
core_idea: In a three-node grid, power intended to move from A to B may instead spill over a secondary path (A to C to B) if the direct line is loaded, and since the operator cannot dictate the exact physical path, it must keep sufficient headroom on all potentially affected lines to prevent overload.
key_points: Resistance on each line changes throughout the day based on local consumption, which changes how power actually flows.
Every transmission line has a maximum power-carrying limit; exceeding it risks equipment failure ('meltdown').
Because flow paths aren't fully controllable, the operator must reserve adequate capacity on every line that could carry a given import, not just the 'intended' direct line.
If sufficient capacity isn't available on the needed paths, imported power may fail to reach its destination even though a contract calls for delivery.
relationships: Line loading/congestion determines whether power can actually follow a direct A-to-B path or is forced onto alternate paths like A-to-C-to-B.
trading_implications: A wheeling deal's physical feasibility depends on grid-wide congestion, not just capacity on the single line nominally being 'rented'.
Congestion risk should be assessed across all plausible flow paths between source and sink, not only the shortest contractual path.
caveats: It is a misunderstanding to assume power takes the contractually intended route; physically it follows least-resistance paths across the network.
